div.head: The text
div.p: A document is a tree of divisions. A division holds headings, then either paragraphs or divisions, never both; headings may stand where the encoding puts them, usually first. Page breaks, notes and gaps may stand between them. The body itself, the document's root, follows the same rule.

Every division and heading has a type, from a closed list, so that a misspelled type fails. A numbered division carries its number as a value in n (49 for a heading XLVIIII; 11a for a chapter after 11), and its number heading keeps the number as written. A unit is a subdivision without a heading of its own, written only where units stand side by side: a division whose text is one unit holds its paragraphs itself.

The paragraphs of a division that holds no divisions are one unit of reception. Where the encoders didn't mark the units, the header says so once, in segmentation with the type inferred-units: for the whole file, when it's the default (default true) or stands alone; or, declared with default false and an id, for the divisions that point to it by decls, where only a few are unmarked among many units. A statement for divisions that none points to is reported.

How far a text has been checked is its curation, given by correction in editorialDecl, its status high, medium, low or unknown, and a paragraph saying how, which TEI requires: the whole text's value is the default; a division or a paragraph that differs points to another correction by decls. Of several corrections, one is the default. decls on the text, the body, a division or a paragraph points only to a correction or a segmentation in the header. What was left out by choice is said once, in samplingDecl; completeness is never stated, but read from the gaps.
